note: Existing-source public educational gallery: CC photos and explicitly credited Bob Harms science/education-only photographs are distinguished. Source labels and arrows are not independent specimen voucher certification.

tiles.heading: 01 · OPEN THE COLLAR
tiles.details: At the INNER blade–sheath junction, look for an actual short membranous ligule approximately 0.5–1 mm long (regional Texas flora/NPS treatment). Narrow blades are often 1–2(3) mm wide. White node hairs are not the ligule. Open the collar and use a 0.5-mm scale; archived gross views do not measure the membrane.
tiles.short: True ligule is a 0.5–1 mm membrane
tiles.status: PUBLISHED 0.5–1 mm MEMBRANE — MEASURED PHOTO MISSING

tiles.heading: 02 · COUNT THE TRIADS
tiles.details: A slender terminal spikelike head is commonly 2–3.5 cm long and carries about 4–8 groups of THREE spikelets. The CENTRAL spikelet has one fertile bisexual floret; TWO lateral spikelets are predominantly staminate, commonly two-flowered. Groups detach as units and may leave a zigzag rachis. These counts are from the Fort Worth/Texas regional treatment, not measured from archived JPEGs.
tiles.short: 4–8 three-spikelet groups on a short axis
tiles.status: HEAD PHOTOS AVAILABLE; SEXED TRIAD DISSECTION MISSING

tiles.heading: 03 · OPEN THE CENTRAL SPIKELET
tiles.details: A mature three-spikelet cluster is generally about 4.5–6 mm in the regional treatment. The central spikelet has basally united, often asymmetric glumes with awnlike extensions commonly 2.5–5 mm; the thin central fertile lemma is described as AWNLESS in the NPS treatment. Never label a glume projection as a fertile-lemma awn. Isolate both central glumes, lemma and palea before placing arrows.
tiles.short: Glume awns are not lemma awns
tiles.status: LITERATURE ANATOMY; BRacts NOT SEPARATELY PHOTOGRAPHED

tiles.heading: 04 · CHECK THE OUTER SPIKELETS
tiles.details: The two lateral spikelets of each cluster are male/staminate and commonly two-flowered, while the central member bears the seed-producing floret. Lateral glumes may be unequal and lobed; the central and lateral bracts must be photographed separately under a 1-mm ruler. Do not mistake the entire three-spikelet fascicle for a single multiflowered spikelet.
tiles.short: Two male companions surround the central fertile one
tiles.status: SEX AND BRAct SEPARATION NOT PIXEL-VERIFIED

tiles.heading: 05 · SEPARATE LOOK-ALIKES
tiles.details: Tobosa (Hilaria mutica) has a coarse perennial stand and short thick SCALY UNDERGROUND rhizomes, not the thin surface-rooting stolons of curlymesquite; both have compact triad-bearing heads. Vine mesquite (Hopia obtusa) has much longer stolons with swollen nodes but a different flowering architecture. Bermudagrass has fingerlike radiating spikes; buffalograss has distinct male and female flowering structures. Do not certify species from dry color or a lone head. Photograph the correct organ: nodal hair tufts on the CREEPING RUNNER, not hairs on the INNER blade/sheath COLLAR. Published regional treatments describe a short true membranous ligule, and some vegetative keys say the collar is largely glabrous.
tiles.short: Tobosa rhizomes below; curlymesquite runners above
tiles.status: COMPARISONS WRITTEN; MATCHED ROOTED PHOTOS NEEDED

tiles.heading: 06 · SURFACE-STOLON CONFIRMATION (LATER)
tiles.details: Curlymesquite is a low perennial, commonly 10–30 cm tall. Trace a slender ABOVEGROUND runner to a rooting node and a second leafy tuft; bearded nodes and narrow leaves that curl as they dry support the ID. A short compact head alone cannot distinguish it from tobosa. Panel 8 physically archives a real uninterrupted ABOVEGROUND stolon connecting a parent leaf tuft to daughter shoots; however its hair-ring and rooted soil node remain unproved.
tiles.short: Creeping native turf: follow a wiry stolon
tiles.status: KNOWN ABOVEGROUND STOLON PHOTO, ROOTING NODE STILL NEEDS PROOF — DEFERRED

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: CURLYMESQUITE / Hilaria belangeri: FIRST examine true inner 0.5–1 mm membranous ligule at an opened leaf blade–sheath junction, not hairs on a distant reddish culm node. SECOND inspect short terminal spikelike heads with 4–8 clustered units, and compare attached and detached papery reproductive parts. The project already has authentic mature heads and detached groups but no calibrated dissection confirming the individual central/lateral members. THIRD examine fine curly leaves, hairy stem nodes and existing photographed thin aboveground stolons. Only LATER pursue exposed roots at stolon nodes. Tobosa has similar grouped heads but coarser habit.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: LIGULE STILL INCOMPLETE: the Bob Harms original photograph labelled ligule/sheath truly shows the sheath and hair placement with size reference, but the FREE membrane edge is NOT clearly exposed. Gently open a verified specimen's INNER blade–sheath junction with 10–20× lens and millimeter scale before labelling the actual 0.5–1 mm membranous lacerate ligule.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: At the INNER blade–sheath junction, look for an actual short membranous ligule approximately 0.5–1 mm long (regional Texas flora/NPS treatment). Narrow blades are often 1–2(3) mm wide. White node hairs are not the ligule. Open the collar and use a 0.5-mm scale; archived gross views do not measure the membrane.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: A mature three-spikelet cluster is generally about 4.5–6 mm in the regional treatment. The central spikelet has basally united, often asymmetric glumes with awnlike extensions commonly 2.5–5 mm; the thin central fertile lemma is described as AWNLESS in the NPS treatment. Never label a glume projection as a fertile-lemma awn. Isolate both central glumes, lemma and palea before placing arrows.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Tobosa (H. mutica) has short, thick SCALY BELOWGROUND rhizomes and no creeping surface stolons, with taller 30–70 cm wiry culms and stiffer, often broader leaves. Both have spikelet fascicles and zigzag stems after seed fall, so the seedhead alone is not proof. Buffalograss (Bouteloua dactyloides) can form short turf but has distinct male and female flowering structures, and bermudagrass (Cynodon dactylon) has a spoke-like digitate inflorescence (3–7 radiating spikes) rather than a solitary short Hilaria flowering axis.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: MATURE ATTACHED HEAD — opened pale spikelet groups on zigzag axis (CC0)
panels.caption: Patrick Alexander photographed two mature Hilaria belangeri flowering heads in Hidalgo County, New Mexico. Compare the compact left head with the more spread-out pale papery groups on the right. Pointed narrow parts and the rachis are visible, but their identity as specific glumes/lemmas and the exact 3-spikelet group boundaries are NOT established by this image alone.

panels.caption: Patrick Alexander's genuine Hilaria belangeri hand-scale close-up shows TWO detached, papery, multi-part mature units. Observe their stout attachment point, projecting narrow parts and apparent branches against the fingers. Photo resolves whole clusters, NOT the exact fertile-versus-staminate three-spikelet arrangement, and this is NOT a true extracted individual lemma close-up.

Look at the successive reddish intact flowering groups on a slender axis; compare with the already archived mature pale clusters and detached papery units. panels.label: GREEN INTACT CURLYMESQUITE FLOWERING HEADS — three real overlapping unshattered spikes (CC0)
panels.caption: Actual green, partly purple unopened-to-maturing curlymesquite heads from New Mexico. Trace the three upright spikes: repeated green papery flowering clusters remain tight and attached. Compare these with the separately archived mature pale fan-shaped units and detached clusters later in the Learner. The three HEADS shown here are NOT the three spikelets inside one microscopic fascicle.

intro: CURLYMESQUITE / Hilaria belangeri: FIRST examine true inner 0.5–1 mm membranous ligule at an opened leaf blade–sheath junction, not hairs on a distant reddish culm node. SECOND inspect short terminal spikelike heads with 4–8 clustered units, and compare attached and detached papery reproductive parts. The project already has authentic mature heads and detached groups but no calibrated dissection confirming the individual central/lateral members. THIRD examine fine curly leaves, hairy stem nodes and existing photographed thin aboveground stolons. Only LATER pursue exposed roots at stolon nodes. Tobosa has similar grouped heads but coarser habit.
memory_rule: CURLYMESQUITE: a short perennial native lawnlike grass often 10–30 cm with little CURLING leaves when dry and relatively small terminal spike-like heads of grouped spikelets. Its best confirmation is a THIN WIRY ABOVEGROUND STOLON physically connecting tufts with hairy rooting nodes (unphotographed in current archive). A short grouped head does NOT distinguish it from tobosa alone. Don't confuse with Bermuda's radiating finger spikes, buffalograss's separate male/female structures, or vine mesquite's long swollen nodes.
safety_note: 17 exact-species curlymesquite photograph records including Bob Harms's real source-labelled dissection, separate flowering fascicles, actual rooted central tuft with connected runners and outer collar/sheath region. Still missing truly peeled-open free 0.5–1-mm ligule edge and confirmed active rooting into soil at every photographed runner node. Expert/mobile arrow overlay and deployed Pages QA pending.
field_rule: Curlymesquite: low turf AND a demonstrated thin ABOVEGROUND stolon connecting tufts, with genuine hairy rooting nodes where soil is exposed, then a short Hilaria-type grouped head. Do not require fully rooted nodes to be visible in one archived reference photograph.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.

Buffalograss (Bouteloua dactyloides) can form short turf but has distinct male and female flowering structures, and bermudagrass (Cynodon dactylon) has a spoke-like digitate inflorescence (3–7 radiating spikes) rather than a solitary short Hilaria flowering axis.
